en.title: Ancient Egypt in the Old Kingdom
en.text:
## A kingdom built around the Nile

The Old Kingdom of ancient Egypt, conventionally dated to approximately 2649–2130 BCE, was the age in which the Egyptian state developed some of its most recognisable institutions and monuments. It is often called the “Age of the Pyramids”, but that phrase captures only one part of a much wider history. The period saw the consolidation of royal government, the growth of a complex administrative system, the development of monumental stone architecture, and the refinement of religious and artistic traditions that continued to shape Egyptian civilisation for centuries.

Egypt’s geography helped make this transformation possible. The Nile provided water, fertile alluvial soil and a transport corridor through an otherwise arid landscape. Its annual inundation renewed agricultural land, while river traffic connected settlements from the Delta in the north to the First Cataract in the south. The river was not simply a backdrop to Egyptian history: it was a central organising force in farming, taxation, communication and political integration.

The Old Kingdom followed the Early Dynastic period, when rulers had established a unified monarchy over Upper and Lower Egypt. The exact chronology and sequence of some early rulers remain subjects of scholarly discussion, and dates used in modern histories are approximate. The Old Kingdom is generally associated with Dynasties Three through Six, although the boundaries vary slightly between chronologies.

## Kingship and the central state

The king stood at the centre of Egyptian political and religious life. Royal authority was expressed through the idea that the ruler maintained maat: the proper order, balance and justice of the world. The king was responsible for sustaining relations between the human community and the gods, protecting the country, organising resources and ensuring that the agricultural cycle continued in an orderly fashion.

This ideology did not mean that the king personally performed every administrative task. A large government coordinated taxation, labour, construction, storage and provincial affairs. Officials recorded resources and supervised activities on behalf of the crown. The vizier was among the most senior administrators, while other officials managed departments, estates, royal works and regional districts known as nomes.

The state’s ability to mobilise labour and materials is visible in its building projects. Stone had to be quarried, transported and shaped; food had to be supplied to workers; and skilled craftsmen, surveyors, scribes and overseers had to coordinate their work. These achievements reveal an organised society with specialised knowledge. They should not be reduced to the idea that pyramids were built by a mysterious technology or by an undifferentiated mass of forced labour. The precise organisation and status of different workforces varied, and evidence from settlements and administrative records has transformed understanding of how royal projects were staffed.

## The pyramid age

The Third Dynasty ruler Djoser is associated with the Step Pyramid complex at Saqqara, designed by the official and architect Imhotep. The monument represents a major development in royal funerary architecture: earlier royal tomb forms were transformed into a monumental structure built in stone. Its surrounding complex included courts, shrines and symbolic architectural features that expressed royal power and the king’s continued existence after death.

The Fourth Dynasty brought the construction of the great pyramid complexes at Giza. Sneferu, who preceded the Giza kings, sponsored major pyramid-building experiments at Meidum and Dahshur. These projects show that pyramid architecture developed through practical experimentation rather than appearing fully formed. Khufu’s Great Pyramid became the largest of the Giza pyramids. His successors Khafre and Menkaure built their own complexes nearby, creating a landscape that joined royal tombs, temples, causeways and subsidiary burials.

The pyramids were not isolated piles of stone. Each belonged to a carefully organised funerary complex. Mortuary temples provided settings for rituals and offerings; valley temples connected the complexes to the Nile and transport routes; causeways linked different parts of the site. Cemeteries for royal relatives and high officials surrounded the royal monuments. Their tombs, often decorated with scenes of agriculture, craft production, hunting, feasting and family life, are among the most important sources for understanding Old Kingdom society.

Pyramid construction also changed over time. During the Fifth and Sixth Dynasties, royal building continued, but pyramid size and design shifted. Some rulers invested heavily in temple decoration and religious texts. The pyramid of Unas, the last king of the Fifth Dynasty, is especially important because its burial chambers contain the earliest known extensive collection of Pyramid Texts. These ritual utterances were intended to assist the deceased king in the afterlife and reveal a sophisticated religious world involving solar, stellar and Osirian ideas.

## Society, work and everyday life

Old Kingdom society was hierarchical, but it was not composed only of kings and peasants. The population included farmers, herders, fishers, craft workers, quarry workers, sailors, soldiers, scribes, priests, administrators and local leaders. Most people lived in settlements along the Nile and depended on agriculture. Grain production supported households, temples and the state. Agricultural surplus could be collected, stored and redistributed to officials, workers and institutions.

Tomb scenes provide vivid evidence of work and social life, although they reflect the perspectives and aspirations of the elite who commissioned them. They show ploughing, sowing, harvesting, animal husbandry, baking, brewing, boat building, metalworking and the manufacture of furniture and jewellery. Such images were not neutral snapshots: they also had religious purposes, representing the resources and activities that the deceased hoped would continue in the next world.

Scribes were particularly important because written records made complex administration possible. Literacy was not universal, and writing was a specialised skill. Administrative documents, labels, seals and inscriptions helped track goods, identify officials and communicate royal authority. The surviving record is uneven: stone monuments and elite tombs are more visible than the lives of ordinary households. Archaeology therefore plays a crucial role in balancing the picture.

## Trade, diplomacy and the wider African world

Old Kingdom Egypt was connected to neighbouring regions through exchange, expeditions and political relationships. The Nile linked Egypt to Nubia to the south, while desert routes connected the river valley to oases and mineral sources. Expeditions sought materials such as copper, turquoise, stone and other resources not readily available in the Nile Valley. Contacts with the Levant and other eastern Mediterranean communities also supplied goods and diplomatic connections.

Nubia was not an empty frontier. Communities to the south had their own histories, economies and political structures. Egyptian activity in Nubia included trade, military campaigns and the establishment of positions that helped secure access to resources and routes. Relations changed across time and could involve cooperation as well as conflict. The archaeological record of Nubian societies is essential for understanding these relationships from more than an Egyptian royal viewpoint.

## Religion, art and the afterlife

Religion permeated public and private life. Temples and royal monuments were places where rituals maintained relationships with the gods, while household practices and personal objects reveal a more varied religious landscape. Beliefs about death and the afterlife developed over centuries. The king’s funerary cult was especially prominent, but non-royal elites also invested in tombs, offerings and representations intended to secure continued existence.

Old Kingdom art followed conventions that communicated identity, status and permanence. Figures were often represented according to established systems of proportion and viewpoint rather than the visual rules of modern realism. Reliefs and statues could portray individuals in idealised forms, while inscriptions identified names, titles and family relationships. These works were not merely decorative; they were active elements in funerary and political life.

## Change and the end of the Old Kingdom

The later Old Kingdom saw changes in the balance of power. Provincial officials and elite families gained influence, and some local tombs became increasingly elaborate. The royal administration did not simply disappear at one moment. Instead, political authority weakened through a combination of developments whose relative importance remains debated.

Changes in Nile flood levels, economic pressures, succession disputes and the growing power of regional elites have all been discussed as possible factors. The evidence does not support a single simple explanation. After the Sixth Dynasty, Egypt entered the First Intermediate Period, during which political authority was divided among competing centres and local rulers exercised greater autonomy.

The end of the Old Kingdom was therefore a transformation, not the disappearance of Egyptian civilisation. Many religious ideas, artistic practices and administrative traditions continued, adapted and re-emerged in later periods. The Middle Kingdom would draw upon the memory of earlier unity while developing new forms of kingship and culture.

## Historical significance

The Old Kingdom matters for more than its pyramids. It demonstrates how an early African state coordinated resources across a long river valley, developed specialised administration, built monumental architecture and created enduring religious and artistic traditions. Its history also shows the importance of interpreting royal monuments alongside settlement archaeology, workers’ communities, provincial cemeteries and evidence from neighbouring societies.

The pyramids remain extraordinary achievements, but they are also historical documents. They tell us about political authority, labour organisation, engineering, religious belief and the ambitions of rulers. The Old Kingdom was not a static civilisation frozen in stone. It was a changing society whose institutions and ideas were continually negotiated by kings, officials, workers, families and communities across the Nile Valley.

## Sources and further reading

- The Metropolitan Museum of Art, “Egypt in the Old Kingdom (ca. 2649–2130 B.C.)”, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/egypt-in-the-old-kingdom-ca-2649-2150-b-c
- The Metropolitan Museum of Art, “Egypt, 8000–2000 B.C.”: https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/ht/02/afe
- The Metropolitan Museum of Art, *The Art of Ancient Egypt: A Resource for Educators*, section “A Summary of Ancient Egyptian History”: https://resources.metmuseum.org/resources/metpublications/pdf/The_Art_of_Ancient_Egypt_A_Resource_for_Educators.pdf

*Chronologies for ancient Egypt are approximate and differ slightly among scholarly publications. This article uses the broad dates adopted by the cited museum resources.*

en.title: The Middle Kingdom of Egypt
en.text:
## Reunification after political division

The Middle Kingdom was a major period of renewal in ancient Egyptian history, conventionally dated to approximately 2030–1640 BCE. It followed the First Intermediate Period, an era when royal authority had weakened and political power was divided among regional centres. The Middle Kingdom began when the Theban ruler Mentuhotep II defeated his northern rivals and reunified Upper and Lower Egypt. His achievement restored a central monarchy, but the state that emerged was not simply a copy of the Old Kingdom. Its rulers, officials, artists and writers reworked older traditions in response to the experience of political fragmentation.

The period is usually associated with the later Eleventh Dynasty and the Twelfth Dynasty, with the Thirteenth Dynasty often included in its later phase. Dates and boundaries differ among Egyptologists. The period’s monuments, literature, sculpture and administrative evidence reveal a civilisation that was both conscious of its past and capable of considerable innovation.

## Mentuhotep II and the restoration of kingship

Mentuhotep II ruled from Thebes in southern Egypt. His reunification of the country was the culmination of a struggle involving competing dynasties and regional authorities. The conflict demonstrated that Egypt’s unity could no longer be taken for granted. Royal power had to be re-established through military success, political alliances, administration and religious legitimacy.

Mentuhotep’s mortuary complex at Deir el-Bahri, on the west bank of Thebes, expressed this renewed kingship through an innovative architectural design. Its terraces, ramps and relationship to the surrounding cliffs created a distinctive monumental setting. The complex combined royal burial, cult activity and the sacred landscape of western Thebes. It also marked a shift in the geography of royal power: Thebes, previously a regional centre, had become the heart of reunification.

The restoration of central government involved more than the king. Officials and provincial leaders had to be integrated into a renewed political order. The monarchy relied on administrators who supervised taxation, agricultural production, transport and the movement of resources. The experience of the First Intermediate Period had made the dangers of decentralisation visible, and later royal ideology placed strong emphasis on stability and order.

## The Twelfth Dynasty and a new political centre

The Twelfth Dynasty brought a particularly strong phase of royal government. Its rulers included Amenemhat I, Senwosret I, Amenemhat II, Senwosret II, Senwosret III and Amenemhat III. The dynasty’s founders consolidated authority and developed a more centralised administration. Amenemhat I established a new royal residence, commonly identified with Itj-tawy, in the region of the Faiyum. Its exact location remains uncertain, but the move placed the royal court in a strategic position between Upper and Lower Egypt.

The Twelfth Dynasty kings sponsored temples, fortifications, irrigation works, expeditions and artistic projects. They also strengthened Egypt’s presence in Nubia. Fortresses along the Nile south of the First Cataract controlled movement and helped secure access to trade routes and resources. These installations were military structures, administrative centres and points of contact between Egyptian officials and Nubian communities.

Senwosret III is especially associated with a more assertive policy in Nubia. His campaigns and fortification programme extended Egyptian control southward, while inscriptions and monuments presented the king as a defender of Egypt’s boundaries. Yet the history of Nubia cannot be understood only through Egyptian military records. Nubian communities had their own political institutions and economic networks, and Egyptian expansion interacted with these societies in complex ways.

## The Nile, agriculture and economic life

Agriculture remained the foundation of Egypt’s economy. The annual Nile inundation deposited fertile silt on cultivated land, while irrigation and basin management helped communities make use of the flood cycle. Grain was central to food supply, taxation and state redistribution. Officials measured fields, recorded yields and supervised the collection and storage of agricultural produce.

The Faiyum region became an important focus of royal and agricultural activity. Its relationship to the Nile and Lake Moeris made it valuable for settlement and cultivation. Projects associated with Middle Kingdom rulers aimed to improve the use of land and water, although the scale and precise effects of individual works remain subjects of scholarly debate.

Trade and expeditions connected Egypt to regions beyond the Nile Valley. Egyptian expeditions travelled to the Eastern Desert and Sinai for minerals and stone, and commercial and diplomatic relations linked the country with the Levant, the Aegean and Nubia. Imported materials and foreign objects found in archaeological contexts demonstrate that Egypt participated in wider networks, even as the state sought to control strategically important routes.

## Literature and the art of the Middle Kingdom

The Middle Kingdom is often regarded as a classical period of Egyptian literature. Texts such as *The Story of Sinuhe*, *The Eloquent Peasant* and *The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor* survive in manuscripts copied at different dates. They explore themes including loyalty, justice, exile, social order, leadership and the relationship between individuals and the state. Their literary sophistication has made them central to the study of ancient Egyptian language and thought.

These works should not be treated as straightforward historical reports. They are literary compositions, shaped by genre, performance and the concerns of the scribal culture that produced and copied them. Nevertheless, they offer valuable evidence for the values and political imagination of the period. The story of Sinuhe, for example, explores the pull of Egypt as homeland and the relationship between an individual and royal authority.

Artistic production also flourished. Middle Kingdom sculpture includes royal images that differ markedly from the idealised youthful representations common in some earlier periods. Certain royal statues, especially those associated with Senwosret III, present the ruler with pronounced facial features and an expression that has often been interpreted as serious or burdened. Scholars debate how far these images should be read as portraits, political statements or conventional representations of kingship.

Private tombs, stelae, jewellery and personal objects reveal a broad range of artistic skill. The quality of carved reliefs and painted decoration demonstrates the work of specialised craftspeople. The survival of objects in tombs provides evidence for social identity, family relationships and religious practice, although elite burials are more visible in the archaeological record than the lives of poorer households.

## Religion and changing ideas of the afterlife

Religious life in the Middle Kingdom drew upon Old Kingdom traditions while adapting them to new circumstances. Osiris became increasingly important in funerary belief, and access to afterlife expectations that had once been closely associated with kingship became more widely expressed among non-royal groups. Coffin Texts, written on the interiors of coffins, developed from earlier funerary traditions and provided spells and guidance for the deceased.

The expansion of funerary texts reflects changes in how individuals and families imagined their prospects after death. It does not mean that all Egyptians enjoyed equal access to elaborate burial practices. Social position and wealth continued to shape the scale of tombs, coffins and offerings. Still, the textual record suggests that religious knowledge and hopes for the afterlife were not confined to the royal household.

Temples remained important institutions. They housed cult images, supported ritual specialists and managed land and resources. Religious institutions were also part of the broader economic and political landscape, connecting royal authority, local communities and the gods.

## The later Middle Kingdom and political change

The later Middle Kingdom, especially the Thirteenth Dynasty, is less clearly understood than the Twelfth. A succession of rulers occupied the throne, and some reigned for relatively short periods. The administrative system continued, but political stability became more fragile. Regional power centres and changing relationships with groups in the eastern Delta contributed to a complex political landscape.

The Second Intermediate Period followed, conventionally dated to approximately 1640–1550 BCE. In parts of northern Egypt, rulers known as the Hyksos established a dynasty based at Avaris. The Hyksos were associated with West Asian connections and were part of a wider pattern of migration, settlement and political change in the eastern Mediterranean. Their rule should not be reduced to a simple story of foreign invasion: the evidence points to a more complicated process involving communities already living in Egypt and new political formations.

The Theban rulers eventually challenged Hyksos power. The conflict culminated in the reunification of Egypt under Ahmose I, who founded the Eighteenth Dynasty and inaugurated the New Kingdom. In this way, the Middle Kingdom’s legacy formed part of the political memory that later rulers used to present themselves as restorers of unity.

## Historical significance

The Middle Kingdom was not merely an interval between the pyramid age and the imperial expansion of the New Kingdom. It was a period of intellectual, artistic and political achievement in its own right. Its rulers restored central authority after a period of division, developed new administrative and military strategies, and sponsored monuments that reshaped the landscape of Thebes and the Nile Valley.

Its literature remains among the most important bodies of writing from ancient Africa. Its art reveals changing ideas about kingship, identity and human experience. Its fortresses and expeditions illuminate Egypt’s relationships with Nubia and neighbouring regions. Above all, the Middle Kingdom demonstrates that Egyptian civilisation was not static: it repeatedly adapted its institutions and cultural traditions to new political and social realities.

## Sources and further reading

- The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Adela Oppenheim, “Egypt in the Middle Kingdom (ca. 2030–1650 B.C.)”: https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/egypt-in-the-middle-kingdom-2030-1640-b-c
- The Metropolitan Museum of Art, “Egypt, 8000–2000 B.C.”: https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/ht/02/afe
- The Metropolitan Museum of Art, “Egypt, 2000–1000 B.C.”: https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/ht/03/afe

*Dates and dynastic boundaries are approximate and vary among Egyptological chronologies.*

en.title: The Kingdom of Kerma
en.text:
## An ancient African power south of Egypt

The Kingdom of Kerma was one of the earliest major states to develop in the Nile Valley south of ancient Egypt. Centred near the Third Cataract of the Nile in what is now northern Sudan, Kerma grew from a regional society into a powerful political and commercial centre during the second millennium BCE. Its history challenges the old assumption that complex state formation in the Nile Valley was driven only by Egypt. The archaeological record shows that Nubian communities developed their own institutions, monumental architecture, craft traditions and long-distance connections.

Kerma takes its modern name from the archaeological site that preserves the remains of its principal urban and ceremonial centre. The culture associated with the kingdom is often divided into Early, Middle and Classic Kerma phases. The chronology is approximate and has been refined as excavations and scientific analyses have expanded. The kingdom was particularly influential during the period when Egypt’s Middle Kingdom and Second Intermediate Period were unfolding.

## The landscape of the Middle Nile

The Middle Nile is not simply a continuation of the Egyptian environment. Its cataracts, stretches of cultivable land, desert margins and river islands shaped settlement and travel in distinctive ways. The Nile provided fertile agricultural zones and a transport route, while the surrounding landscapes supplied livestock, minerals and other resources. Communities could connect with the Red Sea, central Sudan and regions farther south through river and overland routes.

Kerma occupied a strategic position in these networks. It lay south of Egypt and north of important regions of central Africa. Its rulers and merchants could participate in exchange between the Nile Valley and areas beyond it. Cattle were especially important in the economy and in expressions of wealth and status. Agriculture, herding, fishing, hunting and craft production all contributed to the society’s livelihood.

## The rise of Kerma

The settlement at Kerma developed over centuries. Early communities built houses and produced pottery, tools and other objects that reveal a distinctive material culture. Over time, the settlement became more substantial and socially differentiated. Large buildings, cemeteries and specialised craft production indicate the emergence of powerful elites and organised political authority.

Kerma’s rulers were able to mobilise labour for monumental construction and to command resources across a wider territory. The most recognisable structure at the site is the Western Deffufa, a massive mud-brick building associated with religious or ceremonial activity. The Eastern Deffufa and other remains add to the picture of a planned and architecturally distinctive centre. These structures were built using local materials and techniques, demonstrating the sophistication of Nubian construction traditions.

The cemeteries at Kerma are particularly important. Large tumuli, some containing rich burial assemblages, reveal differences in status and the presence of an elite capable of commanding considerable wealth. Cattle remains and other grave goods point to the importance of livestock in social and ritual life. Burial practices changed over time, and archaeologists use these differences to trace the development of political authority and cultural identity.

## Economy and long-distance exchange

Kerma’s economy combined agriculture, animal husbandry, craft production and trade. The Nile’s floodplain supported cultivation, while pastoralism provided meat, milk, hides and social wealth. Cattle had economic and symbolic significance, and their presence in burial contexts suggests that livestock was closely tied to ideas of prestige and authority.

Kerma also participated in exchange networks linking Nubia with Egypt and other regions. Egyptian sources refer to products from the south, including gold, ivory, ebony, incense and animal products. The precise routes and political arrangements varied over time. Some commodities moved through intermediaries, while others were obtained through direct contact, diplomacy or military expeditions.

Archaeological finds show that Kerma was not simply a passive recipient of Egyptian goods. Its craftspeople developed distinctive pottery traditions, including fine red-polished wares with black tops, and produced objects that reflect local aesthetic choices. Imported materials and foreign objects were incorporated into Nubian contexts in ways that reveal selective adoption rather than cultural dependence.

## Kerma and Egypt: trade, diplomacy and war

Relations between Kerma and Egypt were complex. At different times they involved trade, diplomatic contact, competition and warfare. Egyptian rulers sought access to Nubian resources and attempted to control strategic sections of the Nile. Kerma’s rulers, meanwhile, defended their own interests and built power through regional alliances and economic networks.

During the Middle Kingdom, Egypt expanded its control into Lower Nubia and constructed a chain of fortresses along the Nile. These fortresses served military, administrative and commercial purposes. They were designed to monitor movement, secure routes and project Egyptian authority. Their presence demonstrates the strategic importance Egypt attached to Nubia, but it also shows that the region was contested rather than empty.

Kerma’s power continued to grow during periods when Egyptian control weakened. During the Second Intermediate Period, the kingdom became a major force in the Middle Nile region. Egyptian texts and archaeological evidence suggest that Kerma exercised influence over areas to the north and maintained relations with rulers in the eastern Delta. The political situation was fluid, and scholars continue to debate the exact nature of alliances and military cooperation.

The relationship between Kerma and Egypt should not be described only through Egyptian royal inscriptions, which often present southern neighbours in the language of threat or submission. Kerma’s own archaeological record provides evidence of a state with its own political ambitions, ceremonial traditions and material culture. Reading the two records together produces a more balanced account.

## The defeat and absorption of Kerma

The rise of the Egyptian New Kingdom changed the balance of power. Egyptian rulers of the Eighteenth Dynasty launched campaigns southward and eventually conquered Kerma’s territory. The campaigns of Thutmose I and later rulers extended Egyptian control deep into Nubia. Egyptian administration, temples and settlements were established in conquered areas, while local elites were incorporated into new structures of authority to varying degrees.

The conquest did not erase Nubian society. People continued to live in the region, maintain local practices and participate in the changing political economy. Egyptian influence was substantial, but it was adapted through local contexts. Over time, Nubian communities developed new forms of identity and political organisation, and the history of the region continued beyond the end of the independent Kerma kingdom.

The archaeological site of Kerma remained significant after the kingdom’s conquest. Its monuments and cemeteries preserve evidence of the earlier state and help scholars reconstruct a period for which written sources are limited. Excavations have shown that the kingdom’s history was more complex and more independent than older Egypt-centred narratives suggested.

## Archaeology and the recovery of Nubian history

Modern understanding of Kerma depends heavily on archaeology. Excavations have uncovered settlement remains, defensive structures, monumental buildings, cemeteries, pottery workshops and imported objects. These materials provide evidence for economic life, social hierarchy, religious practice and political connections.

Archaeology also raises important questions about interpretation. The presence of Egyptian objects does not automatically mean Egyptian political control. Imported goods can result from trade, diplomacy, gift exchange, warfare or the movement of people. Similarly, similarities in architecture or burial customs must be interpreted in their local context rather than treated as proof that one society simply copied another.

The study of Kerma is part of the broader recovery of ancient Sudanese history. Sudan’s archaeological heritage includes many societies and political traditions that developed along the Nile and beyond it. Kerma’s prominence reminds us that ancient African history cannot be reduced to the history of Egypt, nor can the histories of Egypt and Nubia be separated from one another.

## Historical significance

The Kingdom of Kerma was a major African state with a distinctive political centre, monumental architecture, specialised crafts and long-distance connections. It interacted with Egypt as a trading partner, rival and military opponent, but it was never merely an extension of Egyptian civilisation. Its rulers controlled resources and routes that mattered across the Nile Valley, and its cultural traditions developed in their own right.

Kerma is essential to understanding the deep history of Sudan and the wider African continent. Its remains demonstrate that complex political organisation and monumental building were established in Nubia long before many later kingdoms of the region. The site also offers a corrective to narratives that treat the Nile Valley as a one-way corridor of influence flowing south from Egypt. The history of Kerma reveals a dynamic region in which African societies shaped their own destinies and helped shape the wider ancient world.

## Sources and further reading

- UNESCO, *General History of Africa, Volume II: Ancient Civilizations of Africa*, including the discussion of Kerma, Napata and Meroe: https://unesdoc.unesco.org/
- The Metropolitan Museum of Art, “Egypt, 2000–1000 B.C.”: https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/ht/03/afe
- The Metropolitan Museum of Art, “Egypt, 8000–2000 B.C.”: https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/ht/02/afe
- UNESCO World Heritage Centre, “Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe” (for the later history of Kush in the Middle Nile): https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1336

*The chronology of Kerma and its relationship with neighbouring Nubian cultures continues to be refined through archaeological research. The article distinguishes the Kingdom of Kerma from the later Kingdom of Kush centred first at Napata and later at Meroe.*
